name: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2
aliases: hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type II

clinicalPearls: The axonal form of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, genetically heterogeneous but with mitofusin 2 (MFN2) variants being the most frequent cause
Clinically resembles CMT1 with distal weakness, wasting, pes cavus and distal sensory loss, but onset can be more variable and reflexes may be relatively preserved

The distinguishing feature is on nerve conduction studies: motor conduction velocities are normal or only mildly reduced while compound muscle action potential amplitudes are reduced, reflecting axonal loss rather than demyelination
Palpable nerve hypertrophy is not a feature, in contrast to CMT1A
Inheritance is usually autosomal dominant, though recessive and other patterns occur depending on the causative gene
Some subtypes have distinctive associations such as optic atrophy, vocal cord palsy or a predominantly motor phenotype
Foot drop, frequent tripping and later hand wasting are common functional problems
reference.pathophysiology: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2 is a hereditary axonal (type 2) motor and sensory neuropathy in which the primary defect is degeneration of peripheral nerve axons rather than the myelin sheath. It is genetically heterogeneous, with the most common cause being variants in MFN2, which encodes a mitochondrial outer-membrane GTPase essential for mitochondrial fusion and axonal mitochondrial transport. Impaired mitochondrial dynamics and energy delivery preferentially affect the longest axons, producing a length-dependent, distal-predominant loss of motor and sensory function. Because myelin is relatively spared, conduction velocities remain near normal while response amplitudes fall as axons are lost.
additionalDifferentials: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (in predominantly motor forms)
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies showing reduced motor amplitudes with preserved or near-normal velocities, indicating an axonal process
Genetic panel testing including MFN2 and other CMT2-associated genes
Clinical assessment for pes cavus and distal wasting
Investigations to exclude acquired axonal neuropathies where the picture is atypical
Family evaluation to establish the inheritance pattern
redFlags: Rapid or asymmetric progression suggesting a superimposed acquired neuropathy
Prominent autonomic, respiratory or bulbar features suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Additional signs such as optic atrophy or upper motor neuron features prompting reassessment
Severe sensory ataxia with recurrent injury
reference.prognosis: Progression is generally slow and life expectancy is normal, though disability from distal weakness, deformity and sensory loss accumulates over time; phenotype severity varies with the specific causative gene and variant.
pitfalls: Failing to separate axonal CMT2 from demyelinating CMT1 on nerve conduction studies, which changes the genetic workup
Overlooking a treatable acquired axonal neuropathy by prematurely assuming a hereditary cause
Missing subtype-specific associated features such as optic atrophy
Assuming preserved reflexes exclude a hereditary neuropathy
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
